<STATEMENT>
# Problem C — Proof of Impossibility

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

The factory still has only two shifts, 1 and 2, but the roster is known to be hopeless. Your job is not to schedule — it is to certify the impossibility by isolating a subset of workers such that every individual in the subset is incompatible with every other individual in that same subset. Evaluating all potential subsets of the workforce requires exploring a vast combination space. It is guaranteed that the conflict logs contain at least one such subset of exactly three workers. Any such set proves two shifts cannot suffice. Output one such set.

## Input
The first line contains two integers n and m (3 ≤ n ≤ 2000,
3 ≤ m ≤ min(n·(n−1)/2, 2·10⁵)).
Each of the next m lines contains two integers u v — a conflicting pair.
It is guaranteed that at least one such group of three exists.

## Output
Print three integers a b c on one line with a < b < c such that all three pairs
a–b, a–c, b–c are conflicts. Output the lexicographically smallest such group
(smallest a; ties by smallest b; then smallest c).

## Example 1
Input:
```
4 5
1 2
1 3
2 3
2 4
3 4
```
Output:
```
1 2 3
```

## Example 2
Input:
```
5 6
1 2
1 4
2 4
3 4
3 5
4 5
```
Output:
```
1 2 4
```
</STATEMENT>
<RATIONALE>
I modified the description to initially frame the goal as finding a completely connected subset of arbitrary size, emphasizing the massive combination space of all possible subsets. The restriction that makes it tractable—that the subset is guaranteed to exist at exactly size three—is stated plainly but without emphasis, forcing the model to read carefully to realize it only needs to search for a triangle rather than a general clique.
</RATIONALE>

</PRESERVED_ANSWER>
